explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul, the letter's writer, says the judge is condemning himself "…because you who pass judgment do the same things." It's like me pointing at someone's crumbs while my own apron looks like a crumb parade. Wagging a finger at somebody else gets awkward fast when the same thing is sitting on your own hands.

Not quite, friend. Paul never says anything about reading the law in this verse. The reason he gives is that the one passing judgment does the same things. Keep your eyes on that one, because it's the whole point of the verse.

Good guess, but Paul isn't talking about speed. I could judge a cookie slowly for a whole hour and the verse would still land the same way. The reason is that the judge does the same things (Romans 2:1). Slow or fast, the crumbs are still on both our hands.

Yes, friend. Paul writes, "And we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is based on truth." No guessing and no rumors, just truth. Think of a recipe card with every measurement exactly right. I'd trust that card over my own memory any day.

Close, but this one is true. The verse says, "And we know that God’s judgment against those who do such things is based on truth." So the judgment isn't a guess or a mood. It rests on truth, and Paul says we know it.

Right on the money, friend. Paul says "…God’s kindness leads you to repentance." So the kindness isn't just there to be enjoyed. It's pointing somewhere, and that somewhere is turning around. I've been on the receiving end of that kindness myself, and it got me out of a very dusty place.

Kindness does feel comforting, I'll give you that. But Paul says where it leads, and the word is repentance (Romans 2:4). So God's kindness is walking you somewhere, not just tucking you in. It's a good walk, too.

I see where your head went, friend, since Paul does say riches. But it's the riches of God's kindness, tolerance and patience, not a fat bank account. And the verse says that kindness leads to repentance (Romans 2:4). Think of it as a different kind of wealth, the kind that can't be spent at the store.

That's the word, friend. Paul says the hard and unrepentant heart is "storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath." Nobody is dropping that on this person from outside. The verse says the storing is something he's doing. That's a heavy line, so let's let it sit for a second.

Sorrow is a heavy word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says the person is storing up wrath against himself for the day when God's righteous judgment will be revealed (Romans 2:5). So the blank holds a stronger word than sorrow. Wrath is what's piling up.

Debt is a very grown-up guess, friend, and a pile of bills does stack up fast. But Paul's word here is wrath. He says the person is storing it up against himself for the day God's righteous judgment will be revealed (Romans 2:5). Same piling idea, much heavier thing on the pile.

Yes, friend. For those who keep at doing good and seek glory, honor and immortality, Paul says "He will give eternal life." Notice who does the giving. It's God, and He's the one handing it out. Perseverance means sticking with it, like a baker who keeps showing up even when the dough is being stubborn.

Riches sound nice, friend, but that's not what Paul says here. He says those who keep doing good and seek glory, honor and immortality get eternal life (Romans 2:7). The prize is life, and a lot more than a full cookie jar. Even I'd pick that over a whole planet of chocolate chips.

A new name would be fun, but it's not in this verse. Paul says God will give eternal life to those who persevere in doing good and seek glory, honor and immortality (Romans 2:7). I'm keeping my name, thank you. Papa Dorin has a nice ring to it.

Careful, friend, this one says the Greek gets left out, and Paul doesn't say that. He writes of "…glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek." Everyone who does good gets it, both the Jew and the Greek. So the statement is false, and the Greek is right there in the verse.

Yes, friend, false. The statement leaves the Greek out, but Paul writes of "…glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek." Everyone means everyone, so both get it. That Greek is right there in the verse, and nobody is getting left out of this batch.

That's the reason, friend. Paul puts it plainly: "For God does not show favoritism." Jew or Greek, doing evil or doing good, the same standard holds. There's no VIP section at the front of this bakery line, and I'm glad, because I'd never make it to the front.

That sounds tidy, friend, but Paul never says it. His reason is that "God does not show favoritism" (Romans 2:11). He's saying the Jew and the Greek get the same treatment. He isn't splitting them into separate lines.

explanations.answer: God gives the Jews more time
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but the verse doesn't go there. Paul says "God does not show favoritism" (Romans 2:11). Giving one group extra time would be a kind of favorite, and that's the very thing he rules out. Same bakery, same clock for everybody.

That's it, friend. Paul says all who sin under the law "will be judged by the law." The law is the standard they stand under. Think of me holding my own cookies up against the recipe card. Funny how the card never lies.
I like the optimism, friend. But Paul says that all who sin under the law will be judged by it (Romans 2:12). Sinning and a reward don't go together in that sentence. The word he picks is judged.

Not this time, friend. The verse says all who sin under the law "will be judged by the law." Nothing in it says anyone is forgotten. The word is judged, and Paul is telling us the law is the standard.

Yes, friend. Paul says, "…it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous." It isn't enough to hear the words. They have to be done. That's the difference between owning a cookie cutter and actually pressing it into the dough.

This is the one Paul sets right against the answer, friend. He says, "…it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God." Hearing alone isn't enough. It's the doers who will be declared righteous.

Teachers don't show up in this verse, friend. Paul sets hearers of the law against doers of the law. He says, "…it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous." Even a great teacher like me has to do the thing and not just talk about it.

explanations.answer: The law's work is written on their hearts
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Paul says, "So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts…" These Gentiles don't have the law, but the work of it shows up inside them. That's a lot closer than any piece of paper could get.

explanations.answer: The law's words are written on their doorposts
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but that's not what Paul says. He says the work of the law is written on their hearts (Romans 2:15). He doesn't mention doorposts at all. The writing is on the inside, not out by the front door.

explanations.answer: The law's teaching came down from their elders
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, friend, but these Gentiles don't have the law, so Paul isn't pointing to a teaching handed down. He says the work of the law is written on their hearts (Romans 2:15). The evidence is on the inside, not passed along from somebody else.

That's the word, friend. Paul says, "…their consciences also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them." So inside each of these Gentiles there's a witness, and it's their own conscience. I think that little voice has pointed at my crumbs more than once.

Neighbors would certainly have opinions, friend, but they're not in this verse. Paul says the Gentiles' consciences bear witness (Romans 2:15). The witness is inside, with their own thoughts accusing or defending them.

Prophets are a fine guess, friend, but Paul doesn't bring them up here. He says it's their consciences that bear witness (Romans 2:15). The witness is on the inside, with thoughts that either accuse or defend.

Yes, friend. Paul says God will judge men's secrets "…through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel." So Jesus is the one through whom God judges them. Paul calls it his gospel, meaning the good news he proclaims. Secrets and all, it's in the best hands.
Angels are mighty, friend, but Paul doesn't say that here. He says God will judge men's secrets "…through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel." Jesus is the one named in the verse.
Not the prophets, friend. Paul says God will judge men's secrets "…through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel." The name in the verse is Jesus, and that's what Paul says his gospel proclaims.
